flextools Optimization — Full Benchmark

2026-05-06

This reports presents a comprehensive benchmark of the flextools demand and battery optimization functions, sweeping across key parameters to illustrate their impact on performance and outcomes.

0 · Data & baselines

The simulations in this report use the energy_profiles dataset included in the package, which contains 15-minute data for a full year (2023) of solar production, load, and time-varying prices.
The demand and battery optimization functions take this raw data and construct the necessary input tables for the solvers; these are shown in the next two sections. The battery parameters are set to capacity = 50 kWh and power = 4 kW (for both charge and discharge) for all simulations in this report.

library(lubridate)

# ── Source datasets ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# energy_profiles: full year 2023, 15-min resolution (35 040 rows)
profiles_week <- flextools::energy_profiles |>
  filter(isoweek(datetime) == 18)   # one representative week (672 rows)

profiles_year <- flextools::energy_profiles   # full year (35 040 rows)

# ── Demand optimization datasets ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# price_exported is set to price_imported - 0.05 so it is always lower
opt_demand_week <- demand_opt_data(profiles_week) |>
  mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)
opt_demand_year <- demand_opt_data(profiles_year) |>
  mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)

# ── Battery optimization datasets ─────────────────────────────────────────────
opt_battery_week <- battery_opt_data(profiles_week) |>
  mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)
opt_battery_year <- battery_opt_data(profiles_year) |>
  mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)

# ── Baselines (no optimization) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
base_demand  <- demand_baseline(opt_demand_week)
base_battery <- battery_baseline(opt_battery_week)

# Average import price — used as a λ reference in both demand and battery sections
avg_import_price <- mean(opt_demand_week$price_imported)

Demand dataset

opt_demand_week |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-datetime, names_to = "variable") |>
  dplyr::filter(variable %in% c("price_imported", "price_exported",
                                 "production", "flexible")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(variable = factor(variable,
    levels = c("price_imported", "price_exported", "production", "flexible"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(datetime, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Input data — demand optimization",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bench() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Battery dataset

opt_battery_week |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-datetime, names_to = "variable") |>
  dplyr::filter(variable %in% c("price_imported", "price_exported",
                                 "production", "static")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(variable = factor(variable,
    levels = c("price_imported", "price_exported", "production", "static"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(datetime, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Input data — battery optimization",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bench() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

    round(base_demand$cost, 2),

  `Battery (no battery)` = c(

) |> knitr::kable()

1 · Demand optimization

The optimize_demand() function shifts flexible load in time to meet one of three goals:

opt_objective Solver Description
"grid" / w = 1 QP Minimise squared net power exchanged with the grid
"capacity" QP Minimise squared net power that exceeds grid capacity
"cost" / w = 0 MILP Minimise energy cost (import/export prices)
w ∈ (0, 1) MIQP Weighted combination of both

Key parameters:

  • w — blending weight; w = 1 is pure grid, w = 0 is pure cost.
  • lambda — penalty on load changes between slots. Larger values produce smoother profiles but may sacrifice objective quality.

1.1 · Tradeoff curve: peak reduction vs. energy cost

sweep_d_w <- sweep_demand(
  opt_demand_week,
  w_seq      = W_SEQ_FINE,
  lambda_seq = 0
)
# Express both KPIs as % improvement relative to baseline (positive = better)
tradeoff_d <- sweep_d_w |>
  mutate(
    peak_reduction_pct = (base_demand$peak_from_grid - peak_from_grid) /
                          base_demand$peak_from_grid * 100,
    cost_savings_pct   = (base_demand$cost - cost) /
                          abs(base_demand$cost) * 100
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(peak_reduction_pct, cost_savings_pct),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "pct_improvement"
  ) |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,
    peak_reduction_pct = "Peak-from-grid reduction (%)",
    cost_savings_pct   = "Energy cost savings (%)"
  ))

# Find crossover (where the two curves are closest to equal)
crossover_d <- sweep_d_w |>
  mutate(
    peak_red  = (base_demand$peak_from_grid - peak_from_grid) /
                 base_demand$peak_from_grid * 100,
    cost_sav  = (base_demand$cost - cost) / abs(base_demand$cost) * 100,
    diff_abs  = abs(peak_red - cost_sav)
  ) |>
  slice_min(diff_abs, n = 1)

ggplot(tradeoff_d, aes(w, pct_improvement, colour = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = crossover_d$w,
    linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x     = crossover_d$w + 0.03,
    y     = max(tradeoff_d$pct_improvement) * 0.85,
    label = paste0("Crossover\nw ≈ ", crossover_d$w),
    size  = 3.5, colour = "grey30", hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E07B54", "#4E8098")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Demand optimization: peak reduction vs. energy cost savings",
    subtitle = "Both metrics expressed as % improvement over the unoptimized baseline (λ = 0)",
    x        = "w  (0 = pure cost  →  1 = pure grid)",
    y        = "% improvement vs. baseline",
    colour   = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bench()

Reading the chart: moving w from 0 → 1 trades cost savings for peak reduction. The crossover marks the w where both benefits are equal on a percentage basis. To the right of the crossover, peak reduction outpaces the cost penalty; to the left, cost savings dominate. For cases where only one objective matters, the endpoints are clear: w = 0 for maximum cost savings, w = 1 for maximum peak reduction. A value near the crossover is a reasonable default when both matter equally.

Note on the cost metric: evaluate_cost() measures only grid energy costs (import price × kWh imported − export price × kWh exported). The "cost" optimization objective also includes balancing-market revenues (price_turn_up / price_turn_down), so the grid-energy-cost savings shown here may understate the true economic benefit of w = 0. Conversely, w = 1 (grid) often shows good grid-cost savings as a side effect of aligning demand with local solar production.

1.2 · Lambda vs. energy savings

sweep_d_lam <- sweep_demand(
  opt_demand_week,
  w_seq      = W_SEQ_COARSE,
  lambda_seq = LAMBDA_SEQ
)
max_savings_d <- sweep_d_lam |>
  filter(lambda > 0) |>
  mutate(s = (base_demand$cost - cost) / abs(base_demand$cost) * 100) |>
  pull(s) |> max(na.rm = TRUE)

sweep_d_lam |>
  filter(lambda > 0) |>
  mutate(
    cost_savings_pct = (base_demand$cost - cost) /
                        abs(base_demand$cost) * 100,
    w_lab = paste0("w = ", w)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, cost_savings_pct, colour = w_lab, group = w_lab)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = avg_import_price,
    linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x     = avg_import_price * 1.5,
    y     = max_savings_d * 0.95,
    label = paste0("avg. import price\n≈ ", round(avg_import_price, 3), " €/kWh"),
    size  = 3.2, colour = "grey40", hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = LAMBDA_SEQ[LAMBDA_SEQ > 0],
    labels = as.character(LAMBDA_SEQ[LAMBDA_SEQ > 0])
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "plasma", end = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title    = "Lambda vs. energy savings (demand)",
    subtitle = "Each line is a different w value; larger λ smooths the profile at the cost of savings",
    x        = "λ (log scale)",
    y        = "Energy cost savings vs. baseline (%)",
    colour   = "w"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

λ guidance lambda adds a quadratic penalty on changes in the flexible load between consecutive time slots — it acts as a smoothness regulariser needed for cost optimization to avoid spiky profiles.

  • λ = 0 (default): no smoothness constraint; the solver is free to make sharp load ramps. This gives maximum objective quality but may produce “spiky” profiles that are hard to implement in practice.
  • λ ≈ 0.01 – 0.1: a good first range to try. Profiles become noticeably smoother with only a small sacrifice in cost savings.
  • λ ≥ 0.5: strong smoothing. The flexible load barely moves from its original shape — cost savings shrink toward zero.

A practical starting reference for lambda is the average import price (≈ 0.095 €/kWh in this dataset): at this value, the ramp penalty is comparable in magnitude to the energy price, providing meaningful smoothing without collapsing savings. Recommended range: λ ≈ average import price to 2× average import price.

2 · Battery optimization

The add_battery_optimization() function schedules battery charge/discharge to minimise a weighted objective (cost, grid, or combined):

opt_objective Solver Description
"grid" / w = 1 QP Minimise squared net power exchanged with the grid
"capacity" QP Minimise squared net power that exceeds grid capacity
"cost" / w = 0 MILP or LP (if cycle_cost > 0) Minimise energy cost (import/export prices)
w ∈ (0, 1) QP Weighted combination of both

Key parameters:

Key parameters are the same w and lambda as for demand, plus:

  • cycle_cost (€/kWh cycled) — explicit degradation penalty added to the cost objective. Setting a non-zero value converts the MILP to a pure LP (much faster) and directly limits cycling.
  • charge_eff / discharge_eff — round-trip efficiency losses; when η < 1 the battery internalises losses in the SOC constraints, which also indirectly reduces cycling.

2.1 · Tradeoff curve: peak reduction vs. energy cost

sweep_b_tradeoff <- sweep_battery(
  opt_battery_week,
  w_seq      = W_SEQ_FINE,
  lambda_seq = 0,
  eff_seq    = 1,
  Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
)
tradeoff_b <- sweep_b_tradeoff |>
  mutate(
    peak_reduction_pct = (base_battery$peak_from_grid - peak_from_grid) /
                          base_battery$peak_from_grid * 100,
    cost_savings_pct   = (base_battery$cost - cost) /
                          abs(base_battery$cost) * 100
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(peak_reduction_pct, cost_savings_pct),
    names_to  = "metric",
    values_to = "pct_improvement"
  ) |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,
    peak_reduction_pct = "Peak-from-grid reduction (%)",
    cost_savings_pct   = "Energy cost savings (%)"
  ))

crossover_b <- sweep_b_tradeoff |>
  mutate(
    peak_red  = (base_battery$peak_from_grid - peak_from_grid) /
                 base_battery$peak_from_grid * 100,
    cost_sav  = (base_battery$cost - cost) / abs(base_battery$cost) * 100,
    diff_abs  = abs(peak_red - cost_sav)
  ) |>
  slice_min(diff_abs, n = 1)

ggplot(tradeoff_b, aes(w, pct_improvement, colour = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = crossover_b$w,
    linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x     = crossover_b$w + 0.03,
    y     = max(tradeoff_b$pct_improvement) * 0.85,
    label = paste0("Crossover\nw ≈ ", crossover_b$w),
    size  = 3.5, colour = "grey30", hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E07B54", "#4E8098")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Battery optimization: peak reduction vs. energy cost savings",
    subtitle = "cycle_cost = 0; η = 1; λ = 0",
    x        = "w  (0 = pure cost  →  1 = pure grid)",
    y        = "% improvement vs. no-battery baseline",
    colour   = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bench()

The chart confirms that w = 0 (cost) maximises energy savings through price-arbitrage, while w = 1 (grid) focuses entirely on peak reduction, often at the cost of energy savings. If the primary goal is to reduce the electricity bill, choose w = 0 (or a low w); if the priority is grid relief, choose w near 1.

2.2 · Cycle count

sweep_b_eff <- sweep_battery(
  opt_battery_week,
  w_seq      = W_SEQ_COARSE,
  lambda_seq = 0,
  eff_seq    = EFF_SEQ,
  Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
)
# Order efficiency legend from highest (100%) to lowest (85%)
eff_levels <- paste0("η = ", scales::percent(rev(EFF_SEQ), accuracy = 1))

sweep_b_eff |>
  mutate(eff_lab = factor(
    paste0("η = ", scales::percent(eff, accuracy = 1)),
    levels = eff_levels
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(w, n_cycles, colour = eff_lab, group = eff_lab)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "viridis", end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title    = "Battery total cycles (7-day) vs. w",
    subtitle = "λ = 0; cycle_cost = 0",
    x        = "w  (0 = cost  →  1 = grid)",
    y        = "Equivalent full cycles (7-day total)",
    colour   = "Efficiency"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

Key insight: efficiency and cycle_cost are parameters that influence the battery profile only through the cost objective (w = 0). For the cost objective, round-trip losses make each charge/discharge cycle less profitable, so the optimizer naturally reduces cycling. For the grid and combined objectives, neither efficiency nor cycle_cost enters the objective function. Any reduction in cycles visible for w = 1 or intermediate w values as efficiency drops is simply a side effect of the changed SOC constraints (less energy is stored and delivered per cycle), not a deliberate optimization decision — the battery profile is less aggressive only because the constraints force it, not because the optimizer is trying to save money.

For practical control of cycling, cycle_cost should always be paired with the cost objective. Using the combined or grid objective and hoping that efficiency limits the cycles is not a reliable strategy.

The reduction in cycles for the cost objective with lower efficiency is beneficial from a lifetime perspective, but it comes at a price: a less efficient battery extracts less value from arbitrage. The next section quantifies this cost in terms of energy savings.

# Battery profiles for each efficiency (cost obj., λ = 0, cycle_cost = 0)
profiles_eff_ts <- opt_battery_week |> select(datetime)
for (e in EFF_SEQ) {
  res <- bench_battery(
    opt_battery_week,
    opt_objective = "cost",
    lambda        = 0,
    charge_eff    = e,
    discharge_eff = e,
    cycle_cost    = 0,
    Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
  )
  profiles_eff_ts[[paste0("η = ", scales::percent(e, accuracy = 1))]] <- res$profile
}

profiles_eff_ts |>
  timefully::plot_ts(
    title        = "Battery profiles by efficiency  (cost obj., λ = 0, cycle_cost = 0)",
    ylab         = "Battery power (kW)",
    legend_width = 120
  )
# Focus on cost objective (w=0), η=90% — lambda varies, cycle_cost = 0
sweep_b_cost_opt_lam <- sweep_battery(
  opt_battery_week,
  w_seq      = 0,
  lambda_seq = LAMBDA_SEQ,
  eff_seq    = 0.90,
  Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
)

# Anchored sweep: lambda varies, cycle_cost = 0.02, η=90%
sweep_b_cost_opt_lam_cc02 <- sweep_battery(
  opt_battery_week,
  w_seq      = 0,
  lambda_seq = LAMBDA_SEQ,
  eff_seq    = 0.90,
  cycle_cost = 0.02,
  Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
)

# cycle_cost × efficiency sweep: all EFF_SEQ values, lambda = 0, w = 0
sweep_b_cc_eff <- purrr::map(EFF_SEQ, function(e) {
  sweep_battery_cc(
    opt_battery_week,
    w_seq          = 0,
    cycle_cost_seq = CYCLE_COST_SEQ,
    charge_eff     = e,
    discharge_eff  = e,
    Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
  ) |> mutate(eff = e)
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
sweep_b_cc_eff |>
  mutate(eff_lab = factor(
    paste0("η = ", scales::percent(eff, accuracy = 1)),
    levels = paste0("η = ", scales::percent(rev(EFF_SEQ), accuracy = 1))
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(cycle_cost, n_cycles, colour = eff_lab, group = eff_lab)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "viridis", end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title    = "Cycle count vs. cycle_cost (cost objective, λ = 0)",
    subtitle = "Higher cycle_cost directly penalises cycling in the objective",
    x        = "cycle_cost (€/kWh)",
    y        = "Equivalent full cycles (7-day total)",
    colour   = "Efficiency"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

Note that the cycle count barely decreases with cycle_cost until values around 0.20 €/kWh — which likely exceeds the real battery degradation cost in most deployments (typical Li-ion values are 0.02 – 0.05 €/kWh). This means cycle_cost alone is not very effective at reducing cycles unless set unrealistically high. Its main benefit is the solver speedup it provides (see Section 3).

# Battery profiles for each cycle_cost (cost obj., η = 90%, λ = 0)
profiles_cc_ts <- opt_battery_week |> select(datetime)
for (cc in CYCLE_COST_SEQ) {
  res <- bench_battery(
    opt_battery_week,
    opt_objective = "cost",
    lambda        = 0,
    charge_eff    = 0.90,
    discharge_eff = 0.90,
    cycle_cost    = cc,
    Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
  )
  profiles_cc_ts[[paste0("cc = ", cc)]] <- res$profile
}

profiles_cc_ts |>
  timefully::plot_ts(
    title        = "Battery profiles by cycle_cost  (cost obj., η = 90%, λ = 0)",
    ylab         = "Battery power (kW)",
    legend_width = 120
  )
# Full parameter-space sweep (w × lambda × eff × cycle_cost) on the week dataset
# Used by the overview bar charts at the end of sections 2.2 and 2.3
obj_seq <- c("cost", "0.1", "0.5", "grid")
sweep_b_overview <- purrr::map(c(0, 0.1), function(lam) {
  purrr::map(obj_seq, function(obj_chr) {
    purrr::map(c(1.0, 0.90), function(eff_val) {
      purrr::map(c(0, 0.02), function(cc_val) {
        obj <- if (obj_chr %in% c("grid", "cost")) obj_chr else as.numeric(obj_chr)
        res <- bench_battery(
          opt_battery_week,
          opt_objective = obj,
          lambda        = lam,
          charge_eff    = eff_val,
          discharge_eff = eff_val,
          cycle_cost    = cc_val,
          Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
        )
        tibble::tibble(
          objective  = obj_chr,
          lambda     = lam,
          eff        = eff_val,
          cycle_cost = cc_val,
          n_cycles   = res$n_cycles,
          cost       = res$cost
        )
      }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
    }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
  }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()
sweep_b_cost_opt_lam_cc02 |>
  ggplot(aes(lambda, n_cycles)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#E07B54") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#E07B54") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = avg_import_price,
    linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x     = avg_import_price * 1.15,
    y     = max(sweep_b_cost_opt_lam_cc02$n_cycles) * 0.95,
    label = paste0("avg. import price\n≈ ", round(avg_import_price, 3), " €/kWh"),
    size  = 3.2, colour = "grey40", hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = LAMBDA_SEQ,
    labels = as.character(LAMBDA_SEQ)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Cycle count vs. λ (cost objective, η = 90%, cycle_cost = 0.02 €/kWh)",
    subtitle = "Including a small cycle_cost anchors the baseline and removes MILP solver instability",
    x        = "λ",
    y        = "Equivalent full cycles (7-day total)"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

With cycle_cost = 0.02 included (to anchor the solver in LP mode), the relationship between lambda and cycle count is cleaner and monotonic. Larger lambda consistently reduces cycles by penalising rapid charge/discharge transitions.

# Collect battery power profiles for each lambda (same settings as sweep above)
profiles_lam_ts <- opt_battery_week |> select(datetime)
for (lam in LAMBDA_SEQ) {
  res <- bench_battery(
    opt_battery_week,
    opt_objective = "cost",
    lambda        = lam,
    charge_eff    = 0.90,
    discharge_eff = 0.90,
    cycle_cost    = 0.02,
    Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD
  )
  profiles_lam_ts[[paste0("λ = ", lam)]] <- res$profile
}

profiles_lam_ts |>
  timefully::plot_ts(
    title        = "Battery profiles by λ  (cost obj., η = 90%, cycle_cost = 0.02 €/kWh)",
    ylab         = "Battery power (kW)",
    legend_width = 120
  )

The average import price (≈ 0.095 €/kWh in this dataset) provides an intuitive reference for setting lambda: at this value, the smoothing penalty on a 1 kW ramp per time slot is comparable in magnitude to the energy cost of importing 1 kWh. Values of lambda well below the average import price have limited effect on cycling; values at or above it produce meaningful smoothing. Recommended range: λ ≈ average import price to 2× average import price — this smooths the profile noticeably while retaining most of the energy savings.

sweep_b_overview |>
  mutate(
    lambda_lab = paste0("λ = ", lambda),
    objective  = factor(objective, levels = c("cost", "0.1", "0.5", "grid")),
    eff_cc_lab = paste0(
      ifelse(eff == 1.0, "η = 100%", "η = 90%"),
      ", cc = ", cycle_cost
    ),
    eff_cc_lab = factor(eff_cc_lab, levels = c(
      "η = 100%, cc = 0", "η = 90%, cc = 0",
      "η = 100%, cc = 0.02", "η = 90%, cc = 0.02"
    ))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(objective, n_cycles)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4E8098") +
  facet_grid(lambda_lab ~ eff_cc_lab, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Cycle count across all parameter combinations (1-week dataset)",
    subtitle = "Rows = λ; columns = efficiency × cycle_cost",
    x        = "Objective",
    y        = "Equivalent full cycles (7-day total)"
  ) +
  theme_bench() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

2.3 · Energy savings

sweep_b_eff |>
  filter(w %in% c(0, 0.5, 1)) |>
  mutate(
    cost_savings_pct = (base_battery$cost - cost) /
                        abs(base_battery$cost) * 100,
    objective = w_label(w)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(eff, cost_savings_pct, colour = objective, group = objective)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = EFF_SEQ,
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E07B54", "#9B59B6", "#4E8098")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Energy cost savings vs. round-trip efficiency",
    subtitle = "Positive = cheaper than no-battery baseline; λ = 0; cycle_cost = 0",
    x        = "Round-trip efficiency",
    y        = "Cost savings vs. no-battery baseline (%)",
    colour   = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bench()

Round-trip efficiency losses are now included in the cost evaluation: charging draws B / charge_eff from the grid (more than stored), and discharging delivers only B × discharge_eff back (less than released from the SOC). This means the savings shown already reflect the full energy cost of operating the battery at a given efficiency.

For the cost objective, lower efficiency directly erodes arbitrage profits — the battery draws more from the grid when charging and delivers less when discharging, so the energy-cost saving shrinks as η falls. For the grid objective, efficiency does not enter the objective function, so the optimizer cycles regardless; the savings change stems entirely from the extra grid energy drawn to compensate for losses, not from a deliberate change in strategy.

sweep_b_cc_eff |>
  mutate(
    cost_savings_pct = (base_battery$cost - cost) /
                        abs(base_battery$cost) * 100,
    eff_lab = factor(
      paste0("η = ", scales::percent(eff, accuracy = 1)),
      levels = paste0("η = ", scales::percent(rev(EFF_SEQ), accuracy = 1))
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(cycle_cost, cost_savings_pct, colour = eff_lab, group = eff_lab)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "viridis", end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title    = "Energy savings vs. cycle_cost (cost objective, λ = 0)",
    subtitle = "Efficiency losses included in cost; each line is a different round-trip efficiency",
    x        = "cycle_cost (€/kWh)",
    y        = "Cost savings vs. no-battery baseline (%)",
    colour   = "Efficiency"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

With efficiency losses now included in the cost evaluation, each line shows the true energy savings at a given efficiency — no manual adjustment is needed. Higher efficiency consistently yields better savings because charging losses are smaller. cycle_cost has little effect on the energy savings themselves (the lines are nearly flat), which confirms that its main role is to limit cycling and speed up the solver rather than improve economic performance.

sweep_b_cost_opt_lam_cc02 |>
  mutate(
    cost_savings_pct = (base_battery$cost - cost) /
                        abs(base_battery$cost) * 100
  ) |>

  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#E07B54") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#E07B54") +

  ) +

    labels = as.character(LAMBDA_SEQ)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Energy savings vs. λ (cost objective, η = 90%, cycle_cost = 0.02 €/kWh)",

    y        = "Cost savings vs. no-battery baseline (%)"
  ) +

The savings decline as lambda increases, consistent with the cycle count reduction: smoother charge/discharge profiles exploit the price spread less aggressively. Setting lambda near the average import price still retains most of the energy savings while meaningfully reducing the cycle count — this confirms the λ ≈ average import price recommendation from the previous section.

3 · Computation time

⚠️ This section runs the timing sweep on the full 1-year dataset (35 040 rows) for λ = 0, 0.01, and 0.1. It may take 10–30 minutes to complete on first run; results are cached.

objectives <- c("cost", "0.1", "0.5", "grid")
timing_lam_seq <- c(0, 0.01, 0.1)

# ── Demand timing (1-year dataset, λ = 0 / 0.01 / 0.1) ───────────────────────
timing_demand <- purrr::map(timing_lam_seq, function(lam) {
  purrr::map(objectives, function(obj_chr) {
    obj <- if (obj_chr %in% c("grid", "cost")) obj_chr else as.numeric(obj_chr)
    d   <- demand_opt_data(profiles_year) |>
      mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)
    res <- bench_demand(d, opt_objective = obj, lambda = lam)
    tibble::tibble(
      objective = obj_chr,
      lambda    = lam,
      time_sec  = res$time_sec
    )
  }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()

# ── Battery timing (1-year dataset, λ = 0 / 0.01 / 0.1) ─────────────────────
timing_battery <- purrr::map(timing_lam_seq, function(lam) {
  purrr::map(objectives, function(obj_chr) {
    purrr::map(c(1.0, 0.90), function(eff_val) {
      purrr::map(c(0, 0.02), function(cc_val) {
        obj <- if (obj_chr %in% c("grid", "cost")) obj_chr else as.numeric(obj_chr)
        d   <- battery_opt_data(profiles_year) |>
          mutate(price_exported = price_imported - 0.05)
        res <- bench_battery(d, opt_objective = obj, lambda = lam,
                             charge_eff = eff_val, discharge_eff = eff_val,
                             cycle_cost = cc_val,
                             Bcap = BCAP, Bc = BC, Bd = BD)
        tibble::tibble(
          objective  = obj_chr,
          lambda     = lam,
          eff        = eff_val,
          cycle_cost = cc_val,
          time_sec   = res$time_sec
        )
      }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
    }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
  }) |> purrr::list_rbind()
}) |> purrr::list_rbind()

3.1 · Demand computation time

timing_demand |>
  mutate(
    lambda_lab = factor(paste0("λ = ", lambda),
                        levels = paste0("λ = ", timing_lam_seq)),
    objective  = factor(objective, levels = c("cost", "0.1", "0.5", "grid"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(objective, time_sec)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4E8098") +
  facet_grid(lambda_lab ~ ., scales = "fixed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Demand computation time by objective and λ (1-year dataset)",
    subtitle = "'cost' with λ = 0 uses MILP — expect longer runtimes",
    x        = "Objective",
    y        = "Time (seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_bench()

3.2 · Battery computation time

timing_battery |>
  mutate(
    lambda_lab = factor(paste0("λ = ", lambda),
                        levels = paste0("λ = ", timing_lam_seq)),
    objective  = factor(objective, levels = c("cost", "0.1", "0.5", "grid")),
    eff_cc_lab = paste0(
      ifelse(eff == 1.0, "η = 100%", "η = 90%"),
      ", cc = ", cycle_cost
    ),
    eff_cc_lab = factor(eff_cc_lab, levels = c(
      "η = 100%, cc = 0", "η = 90%, cc = 0",
      "η = 100%, cc = 0.02", "η = 90%, cc = 0.02"
    ))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(objective, time_sec)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4E8098") +
  facet_grid(lambda_lab ~ eff_cc_lab, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(
    title    = "Battery computation time by objective, λ, efficiency, and cycle_cost (1-year dataset)",
    subtitle = "'cost' with λ = 0 and cycle_cost = 0 uses MILP; cycle_cost > 0 switches to LP (faster)",
    x        = "Objective",
    y        = "Time (seconds)"
  ) +
  theme_bench() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

Key takeaways from the computation time analysis:

  • Grid optimization is always fast — regardless of dataset length, lambda, efficiency, or cycle_cost, the QP solver (OSQP) solves the grid objective in a fraction of a second. No parameter tuning is needed to keep it quick.

  • For cost optimization, cycle_cost is the most impactful parameter — with cycle_cost = 0, the cost objective requires a MILP (HiGHS) that scales poorly with dataset length. Setting even a small cycle_cost > 0 (e.g. 0.02 €/kWh) converts the problem to a pure LP, recovering solve times comparable to the grid objective. This is the recommended approach for cost optimization in production.

  • For combined objectives, lambda is the main lever — with lambda = 0, combined objectives already use a QP (fast), but adding lambda > 0 on a combined objective provides limited practical benefit: the grid component already smooths the spiky profile that lambda would otherwise target. Using lambda makes most sense when w = 0 (pure cost) and the goal is to reduce profile spikiness without fully switching to the grid objective.

  • Efficiency (η < 1) has a negligible effect on computation time — efficiency changes the SOC constraints but does not alter the solver type. The timing difference between η = 100% and η = 90% is minimal.

4 · Summary and guidelines

The table below gives a quick parameter reference. The guidelines that follow summarise the recommended use of each objective.

tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c(
    "w (combined weight)",
    "w (combined weight)",
    "λ (ramping penalty)",
    "λ (ramping penalty)",
    "λ (ramping penalty)",
    "cycle_cost (battery)",
    "cycle_cost (battery)",
    "Efficiency (battery)",
    "Efficiency (battery)",
    "Solver (cost, λ=0, cc=0)",
    "Solver (cost, λ>0 or cc>0)",
    "Solver (grid / combined)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    "0 (cost)", "1 (grid)",
    "0", "0.01–0.1", "≥ 0.5",
    "0", "> 0 (e.g. 0.02)",
    "< 1 (e.g. 0.9)", "= 1",
    "MILP (HiGHS)", "LP or QP (OSQP)", "QP (OSQP)"
  ),
  Effect = c(
    "Minimise energy cost; may increase peak; MILP solver",
    "Minimise peak; may increase cost; fast QP solver",
    "No smoothing; sharpest profile changes",
    "Recommended: smooth profiles, minor objective loss",
    "Heavy smoothing; profile barely moves, savings near zero",
    "No cycling penalty; MILP solver for cost objective",
    "Reduces cycles; switches to LP (faster than MILP)",
    "Fewer cycles for cost obj.; losses modelled in SOC constraints",
    "Efficiency not modelled in constraints",
    "Slow (especially for long datasets)",
    "Fast (LP or continuous relaxation)",
    "Fast; scales well with time-series length"
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Quick reference: parameter effects")
Quick reference: parameter effects
Parameter Value Effect
w (combined weight) 0 (cost) Minimise energy cost; may increase peak; MILP solver
w (combined weight) 1 (grid) Minimise peak; may increase cost; fast QP solver
λ (ramping penalty) 0 No smoothing; sharpest profile changes
λ (ramping penalty) 0.01–0.1 Recommended: smooth profiles, minor objective loss
λ (ramping penalty) ≥ 0.5 Heavy smoothing; profile barely moves, savings near zero
cycle_cost (battery) 0 No cycling penalty; MILP solver for cost objective
cycle_cost (battery) > 0 (e.g. 0.02) Reduces cycles; switches to LP (faster than MILP)
Efficiency (battery) < 1 (e.g. 0.9) Fewer cycles for cost obj.; losses modelled in SOC constraints
Efficiency (battery) = 1 Efficiency not modelled in constraints
Solver (cost, λ=0, cc=0) MILP (HiGHS) Slow (especially for long datasets)
Solver (cost, λ>0 or cc>0) LP or QP (OSQP) Fast (LP or continuous relaxation)
Solver (grid / combined) QP (OSQP) Fast; scales well with time-series length

Grid optimization (w = 1) Use this when the primary goal is to reduce peak demand from the grid and the energy cost is a secondary concern. The solver is always fast (QP), parameters like lambda, cycle_cost, and efficiency have no impact on computation time, and the resulting profile is already smooth. There is no need to tune lambda for this objective.

Cost optimization (w = 0) Use this when minimising the energy bill is the primary goal. Key recommendations:

  • Always set cycle_cost > 0 (e.g. 0.02 €/kWh) — this switches the MILP to an LP (dramatically faster) and is economically meaningful as a degradation cost.
  • Set lambda ≈ average import price to smooth the charge/discharge profile without sacrificing significant savings. Together, cycle_cost and lambda give good control over the cycle count vs. savings tradeoff.
  • Lower round-trip efficiency reduces cycles and savings proportionally; use the actual measured η for realistic results.

Combined optimization (w ∈ (0, 1)) Use this when both cost and peak objectives matter. The crossover w (where both metrics are equal on a percentage basis) is a natural starting point. Note that:

  • The grid component already smooths the profile, making lambda largely redundant for combined objectives.
  • Cycling behaviour is dominated by the grid component even at moderate w values, so cycle_cost remains the recommended tool for limiting cycles.
  • The solver is a fast QP for all w > 0 (with or without lambda), so computation time is not a concern.
